pedagogy.summary: This is the CAUSAL explanation of Moon phases at primary grain, building on the earlier observational topic (that the Moon's shape changes over ~a month). Three linked ideas: (1) the Moon orbits Earth roughly once every 28-30 days; (2) the Moon makes NO light of its own — it reflects sunlight, so the Sun always lights up one half of it; (3) phases are caused by how much of that lit half we can see from Earth as the Moon moves around us. The crucial and hard idea is that phases are NOT the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon — they are a viewing-angle effect. Teach with a lit ball orbiting the child's head so the child sees the lit fraction change from their own vantage point.
bestPractices: Use the classic ball-and-lamp model: a single lamp (Sun) lights one half of a ball (Moon) at all times; the child holds the ball at arm's length and slowly turns around, watching how much of the lit half faces them — reproducing new, crescent, half, gibbous, full from their own point of view.
Make the reflected-light idea explicit and testable first: half the Moon is ALWAYS lit by the Sun; what changes is only how much of that lit half we see — not how much is lit.

Directly confront the Earth's-shadow misconception: show that in most phases the Earth is not between the Sun and Moon at all, so its shadow is not on the Moon; reserve Earth's shadow for the separate rarer event (a lunar eclipse), which is NOT the cause of ordinary phases.
Link the phase cycle to the orbit period the child already met: one trip of the Moon around Earth ≈ one month ≈ one full phase cycle, connecting motion to appearance.
Couple the space view (Moon orbiting Earth, lit half fixed toward the Sun) with the Earth view (what the Moon looks like tonight) so the child maps position-in-orbit to shape-in-the-sky.
keyRepresentations: Ball (Moon) + single lamp (Sun) + child's head (Earth) — the canonical phases model seen from the child's own viewpoint
Half-lit sphere: the Sun always lights exactly one hemisphere of the Moon (fixed toward the Sun)
Coupled dual view: overhead space view of the Moon at 8 orbit positions PLUS the matching Earth-view shape for each position
Phase wheel / strip: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning … mapped around the orbit
The terminator on the Moon (the line between its lit and unlit halves) as the boundary we see cutting across the disc
commonMisconceptions: Believing phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the single most common and persistent error) — rather than by our changing view of the lit half.
Thinking the Moon produces its own light, rather than reflecting the Sun's.
Believing clouds, or an object passing in front, cover the Moon to make the phases.
Thinking only part of the Moon is lit at any time (not realising a full hemisphere is always lit; what changes is our viewing angle).
Confusing the ordinary monthly phase cycle with a lunar eclipse (which IS Earth's shadow, but rare) — merging two different phenomena.
Assuming the Moon is only visible at night, or that a new moon means the Moon has 'gone away'.

learn.summary: Teaches the causal explanation of Moon phases for ages 7-9: the Moon orbits Earth about once a month, makes no light of its own but reflects sunlight (so one half is always lit by the Sun), and the phases we see are caused by how much of that lit half faces us from Earth as the Moon moves around us. The central, hard idea is that phases are a viewing-angle effect, NOT the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (that rarer event is a lunar eclipse). The canonical activity is a lit ball (Moon) orbiting the child's head (Earth) under a single lamp (Sun) so the child watches the lit fraction change from their own vantage point; screen models and a reference diagram support and extend this.

activities.title: Ball-and-lamp: orbit the Moon around your own head
feedback: If a learner says part of the Moon has 'gone', ask them to find the dark half with their finger — it is still there, just turned away from them.
If they say the light changes, pause the ball: the lamp still lights about one half, the same amount as before; only the learner's viewing angle changed.

Prompt: can you make a thin crescent by holding the ball ALMOST between you and the lamp, just off to one side? Note that if the ball is directly between you and the lamp you see only its dark side — a new moon — and nudging it aside reveals a thin bright sliver. Where is the bright side pointing now?

If a shadow creeps across the ball at the 'full' position, that is your own head's shadow — raise the ball a little so it misses. It is not the cause of the phases; the lit half always stays facing the lamp, which is why we keep the ball above our shadow.
activities.rationale: Phases depend on the relationship between Sun-light direction, the Moon's orbital position, and the Earth viewpoint; moving the Moon and watching the visible lit fraction change makes the cause-to-appearance link concrete from the child's own vantage point. Raising the ball avoids the learner's head casting a shadow that could be mistaken for the cause.
sourceClaims: The ball-and-lamp model viewed from the learner's own vantage point is the canonical method for teaching Moon phases as a viewing-angle effect.

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, shine a single lamp (the Sun) on a ball (the Moon); notice one half of the ball is always bright and the other half dark.
Hold the ball at arm's length and slightly above head height (so your own shadow does not fall on it), stand with your head as Earth, and slowly turn all the way around so the ball orbits your head.

As you turn, watch how much of the bright half you can see and name the views you pass through: all of it (full), half the disc lit (quarter), a thin sliver (crescent), or none at all (new) — these appear at different points as you rotate, not only at the quarter-turns.
Say aloud for one position: 'The Moon is still fully half-lit by the lamp — I am just seeing more / less of the bright side from here.'
Point to where the dark side is pointing when you see a crescent, to confirm nothing is covering the Moon.
activities.intendedInsight: Phases are caused by our changing view of the always-half-lit Moon as it orbits, not by anything covering or shadowing it.

activities.title: Does the Moon make its own light?
feedback: If the learner expected the ball to stay lit, connect it to the lamp-off result: no Sun, no reflected light, no glow.
Reinforce: the Moon shines by bouncing back the Sun's light, like a brightly lit wall, not by making its own light like a lamp.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that the Moon is its own light source with a model: the ball, like the Moon, makes no light of its own, so switching off the lamp shows what happens to an object that only reflects light. A switchable light source (lamp or an on/off control in a screen model) makes this dependence visible. It models the Moon's dependence on the Sun rather than testing the real Moon.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Put the ball where you can see its bright and dark halves.
Predict what happens to the ball if the lamp is switched off.
Switch off the lamp and observe: the ball goes dark, or only stays dimly visible from any other light leaking into the room, because it makes no light of its own.
Explain in a sentence where the Moon's glow comes from, using the word 'reflect'.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon produces no light of its own; it shines only by reflecting the Sun's light, so with no Sun there is nothing to see.

activities.title: Where is Earth's shadow really? Separating phases from eclipses
feedback: If a learner explains a crescent as Earth's shadow, trace the shadow direction with them and show it misses the Moon entirely.
Clarify: a lunar eclipse only happens at certain full-moon line-ups, not every month, so it cannot be the monthly phase cause.
A 'show Earth's shadow' toggle (in a screen model) or a torch casting the real shadow (with the ball) can make the shadow direction visible for each position.
activities.rationale: The Earth's-shadow belief is the most common and persistent phase misconception; having the learner locate where the shadow actually falls lets them rule it out themselves, rather than being told it is wrong.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: For an ordinary crescent or half phase, work out where the Sun is, where the Moon is, and where Earth's shadow would stretch (straight away from the Sun).
Check whether Earth's shadow actually falls on the Moon in that position — in ordinary phases it points off into empty space, nowhere near the Moon.
Describe the special, rare line-up when Earth is EXACTLY in line between the Sun and the full Moon, so the shadow does reach the Moon — name this a lunar eclipse.
Write one sentence stating what causes ordinary phases and one sentence stating what causes a lunar eclipse, keeping them separate.
activities.intendedInsight: In ordinary phases Earth's shadow does not touch the Moon, so phases cannot be caused by it; Earth's shadow on the Moon is a separate, rare event (a lunar eclipse).

activities.title: Map position in orbit to shape in the sky (coupled dual view)
feedback: If the learner memorises the sequence without the cause, ask them to justify a shape by pointing to where the lit half faces.
Link back to the ball-and-lamp: the overhead space view is the same situation seen from above instead of from the learner's eyes.
activities.rationale: Coupling the space view (lit half fixed toward the Sun) with the Earth view (tonight's shape) lets the learner map orbit position to appearance and ties the phase cycle to the orbit period. A draggable Moon with a live-updating Earth-view window makes the mapping dynamic; stepping the model works as an alternative.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth'.

The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Look at an overhead 'space view' showing the Moon at several positions around Earth, with its lit half always facing the Sun.
For a chosen orbit position, predict the shape you would see from Earth before checking the matching 'tonight's sky' Earth-view.

Drag or step the Moon around the orbit and watch the Earth-view shape change: full when the Moon is on the far side from the Sun, thinning to a crescent as it swings towards the Sun, vanishing at new moon.

Connect the repeating phases to the Moon’s motion around Earth: a full phase cycle is about a month. The orbital period relative to the stars is slightly shorter than the phase cycle because Earth is also moving around the Sun.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon’s position relative to the Sun and Earth determines the phase seen from Earth. Both the orbital period and phase cycle are roughly a month, but they are not exactly the same period.

activities.title: Fly to Earth's surface and look up (spatial extension)
feedback: If the shapes seem to disagree, return to the space view and check which part of the lit half is turned towards the Earth viewpoint.
activities.rationale: The Sun-Earth-Moon geometry is genuinely spatial, and moving between a space view and a stood-on-Earth view can strengthen the link between orbit position and observed shape. This enriches the 2D mapping; the essential cause-to-appearance idea is already carried by the ball-and-lamp and the dual view.
sourceClaims: UK National Curriculum Year 5 (Earth and space) requires pupils to 'describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth'.
learnerActions: Using a 3D model, orbit the camera to view the Sun-Earth-Moon system from space, keeping the Moon's lit hemisphere always facing the Sun.
Drop the camera down to stand on Earth's surface and look up at the Moon for the current orbit position.
Compare the shape you see looking up with the lit half shown in the space view, and explain why they match.
activities.intendedInsight: Standing on Earth and looking up connects the Moon's orbital position directly to the shape you would actually see in the sky.

activities.title: Reference diagram and recap of the 8 phases
feedback: Use this as a recap after the hands-on work, not as the first teaching: a static diagram shows the pattern but does not let the learner test why the visible fraction changes, so return to the ball or dual view if a learner recites names without the cause.
If a learner labels the full-moon position 'eclipse', remind them an eclipse needs the special Sun-Earth-Moon line-up.
activities.rationale: A labelled static diagram is a useful reference and consolidation for the sequence and vocabulary, and reveal-the-label prompts aid recall; because it does not recompute the visible fraction as the learner moves the Moon, it best supports review after the mechanism has been built.
learnerActions: Study a labelled diagram of the eight phase positions around the orbit: new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent.
Reveal or state the name and Earth-view shape for each position.
On the full-moon position, note that it is usually a full phase and only a lunar eclipse at the rare special alignment, keeping phase and eclipse distinct.
Order the phases into the correct cycle and say which way the lit part grows (waxing) and shrinks (waning).
activities.intendedInsight: The named phases form a repeating cycle around the orbit, and the full-moon position is normally just a phase, not an eclipse.

activities.title: Check and explain: two-tier phase questions
feedback: Full understanding: the Moon reflects sunlight (always half-lit), phases are the changing amount of that lit half we see as it orbits monthly, and ordinary phases are separate from the rare lunar eclipse.

Partial: knows the Moon reflects sunlight and orbits Earth but still reaches for Earth's shadow or cannot say why the lit amount we see changes — return to the ball-and-lamp and the shadow-direction task.
Gap: attributes phases to Earth's shadow and/or thinks the Moon makes its own light — reteach reflected light and the orbit-position-to-shape mapping.
activities.rationale: A two-tier true/false-with-why question discriminates because the shadow explanation sounds plausible and is stated confidently by those who hold it, while the 'why' tier also surfaces the self-light misconception. This checks understanding rather than building the spatial-causal idea, so it belongs alongside the hands-on activities. Note that recognising a correct answer in options does not, by itself, demonstrate the learner can produce the explanation, so the 'why' tier matters.
sourceClaims: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight and its phases result from our changing view of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth; the Earth's-shadow explanation of phases is a well-documented, persistent misconception distinct from a lunar eclipse.
learnerActions: Answer whether this statement is right: 'The crescent happens because Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon' — then explain WHY in your own words.
Choose what causes Moon phases from options that include the Earth's-shadow idea as a tempting wrong answer, and justify your choice.
Match each orbit position to the shape seen from Earth, and put the phases in order.

Answer the probes: where does the Moon's glow come from if it makes no light? At a thin crescent, is the rest of the Moon gone or just not lit towards us? How is a lunar eclipse different from a crescent? How long is one orbit and phase cycle?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to reject the shadow explanation and give the reflected-light, viewing-angle reason shows understanding rather than only memorised phase names.

constraints: This causal topic builds on observations that the Moon’s phases repeat about monthly. Use about a month at this age without equating the exact periods: the orbit relative to the stars is about27.3days, while the phase cycle is about29.5days; children need not memorise these precise figures here.

Keep the single light source fixed so that about one half of the Moon is always lit. With a nearby lamp it is slightly less than half, but the lit amount stays the same as the ball moves. The lesson is undermined if learners think the amount LIT changes rather than the amount SEEN.

In the hands-on ball-and-lamp, have learners raise the ball slightly above their own head so their head's shadow does not fall on it at the full position, which would otherwise mimic and reinforce the Earth's-shadow misconception.

Address the Earth's-shadow misconception by having learners locate where the shadow actually falls, and clearly name the lunar eclipse as the separate, rare shadow event — do not let the two phenomena merge.
A static diagram supports recap and vocabulary but does not let learners vary the viewing angle themselves, so use it after the hands-on or dynamic work, not as the primary teaching.

A quiz checks facts and confronts the misconception but does not itself build the spatial-causal understanding; pair it with construction/explanation activities. Recognising a correct option is not the same as producing the explanation.
3D fly-to-surface views are enriching for the spatial link but are not required; the cause-to-appearance mapping is fully carried by the ball-and-lamp plus a space-view/Earth-view pairing.

Interactive features named here (draggable Moon, live Earth-view window, show-shadow toggle, Sun on/off switch) are optional ways to make the mechanism visible; equivalent hands-on versions with a ball, lamp and torch work too.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the original (the NGSS/misconception claim and the ball-and-lamp pedagogy-consensus claim); treat their support as unverified. Only the DfE National Curriculum Year 5 claim is marked verified:true.

Original source claims support the teaching principles (reflected light, viewing-angle cause, shadow misconception, curriculum coverage) but do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any specific medium; efficacy wording is kept as 'may/can/intended'.

The original framing that a conversation/in-role format 'cannot make the viewing-angle effect felt' and that 3D 'adds nothing essential' has been softened to scoped affordance claims, not established universal limits.

Original lists the standard 28-30 day orbit figure and 'about a month' for the phase cycle; the sidereal orbital period (~27.3 days) and synodic phase cycle (~29.5 days) differ slightly. At this age 'about a month' is acceptable, but note the distinction if precision is later needed.

Added a practical safeguard to the ball-and-lamp activity: raise the ball above head height so the learner's own shadow does not fall on it at the full position (otherwise it can be mistaken for Earth's shadow and reinforce the very misconception being addressed).

The reference-diagram activity's sourceClaims were set to [] because its rationale concerns the recall/consolidation affordance of a static diagram, which none of the available source claims directly supports (the DfE claim is about describing Moon movement, a topic-level match only).

The original 'terminator' representation and the 'Moon only visible at night' misconception are not separately carried into these activities; the underlying always-half-lit idea and the 'gone away' belief are retained. Add them if fuller coverage is wanted.
One error-pattern entry references a reteach prerequisite id; this is internal routing metadata and is not reproduced in learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: If the Moon makes no light of its own, where does its glow come from?
When we see a thin crescent, where is the rest of the Moon — gone, or just not lit towards us?
How is a lunar eclipse different from an ordinary crescent phase?
How long does the Moon take to go once around the Earth and back to the same phase?
assess.correctAnswer: No — Earth's shadow is not what causes the ordinary phases. The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight, so the half of the Moon facing the Sun is always lit. As the Moon orbits Earth (about once a month), we see different amounts of that lit half from where we stand — sometimes all of it (full), sometimes a sliver (crescent), sometimes none (new). That changing VIEW of the lit half, not Earth's shadow, makes the phases. (Earth's shadow does fall on the Moon occasionally — but that is a rare, separate event called a lunar eclipse.)

errorPatterns.pattern: the Moon's phases are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a lamp and a ball: the lit half always faces the lamp, and walking the ball around 'Earth' reproduces every phase with NO shadow involved; name the rare eclipse as the real shadow event.
errorPatterns.distractor: The phases happen because the Earth's shadow covers up part of the Moon.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child explains the crescent or half moon as Earth's shadow covering part of the Moon

errorPatterns.pattern: the Moon makes its own light / glows by itself
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a ball in a single beam — one side bright, one dark; the Moon shines only by bouncing back the Sun's light.
errorPatterns.distractor: The Moon shines because it makes its own light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats the Moon as a light source rather than a reflector of sunlight

errorPatterns.pattern: at new moon the Moon has gone away or disappeared
errorPatterns.nextMove: The Moon is still there — its lit side is facing away from us, so the side we see is dark; it hasn't gone anywhere.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child thinks the Moon leaves the sky at new moon

responseLevels.gap: Attributes phases to Earth's shadow and/or thinks the Moon makes its own light.
responseLevels.full: Explains the Moon reflects sunlight (always half-lit), that phases are the changing amount of that lit half we see as it orbits monthly, and separates ordinary phases from the rare lunar eclipse.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the Moon reflects sunlight and orbits Earth, but still reaches for Earth's shadow to explain the phase shapes, or can't say why the lit amount we see changes.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Some people think the Moon's phases — like the thin crescent — happen because the EARTH'S shadow falls on the Moon and hides part of it. Is that right? If not, what really causes the phases? And does the Moon make its own light? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The Earth's-shadow explanation is the single most common phase misconception and sounds plausible, so a child who holds it states it confidently. A child who understands the geometry rejects the shadow and explains phases as seeing different amounts of the always-lit half as the Moon orbits. The 'why' tier also catches the belief that the Moon is its own light source.
